title: The iconostasis
hookLine: the Orthodox icon screen, both veil and window

cards: At the far end of an Orthodox church, right where the long walk would reach the altar, there's a wall. Not plain stone. A wall of faces.
Christ on one side of a central doorway; on the other, Mary, holding him as a child. Angels on the side doors. Saints in rows, gold behind every head.

Candles flicker, and in that light the faces seem to shift. Then, at a certain moment in the service, the central doors swing open: the altar, light, a priest moving. A little later, the doors close again.

teach.h: A VEIL BEFORE THE HOLIEST PLACE.
teach.b: The icon wars of day eight hundred one were fought over faces like these. The iconostasis is the screen of icons between the nave, where the people are, and the sanctuary, where the altar is.
Orthodox Christians describe it two ways at once. First, a veil. In the temple in Jerusalem, a veil hung before the holiest place.

Matthew says that when Jesus died, "behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom." So the screen still marks a threshold: something holy is behind it, and it isn't simply put on display.
Second, a window. In the Orthodox understanding an icon isn't decoration.

teach.h: A WINDOW: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.
teach.b: Colossians calls Christ "the image of the invisible God," and the Greek word there for image is eikon.
Orthodox Christians teach that because God became visible in Christ, his face may be painted, and an icon opens onto the one it shows. So the congregation isn't facing a wall.
It's facing a crowd: Christ, Mary, the saints, looking back. Third, the doors.
The central ones, called the royal or holy doors, open and close during the liturgy. The gospel book passes through them. At communion, the cup is brought out through them.

teach.h: THROUGH A GLASS, DARKLY; THEN FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: Paul put that rhythm into one sentence: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Other churches arrange this space in other ways, some with the altar in full view.
The Orthodox screen holds both halves of Paul's line in one wall.

how: In Orthodox churches an iconostasis stands between the nave and the altar; worshipers light candles before its icons and venerate them, and the central doors open and close at set moments of the Divine Liturgy.

games.q: you're standing before an icon screen, and the central doors are closed. what is the screen doing?
o: hiding and showing at the same time
games.why: Orthodox Christians call it both veil and window: it marks off the altar, and its faces look straight back at you.

practice: Find a photo of an icon screen, or picture one, and let your eyes rest on a single face and stay there. Notice the doors in the middle, closed for now; you don't have to know what's behind them.
If you pray, say Paul's words quietly, now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face, or simply let the face look back at you while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: The iconostasis. The Orthodox screen of icons between the people and the altar: a veil that hides, and a window of faces.

orig.note: Greek: image. The word in Colossians 1:15, "the image of the invisible God."

carryVoice: Your line: veil and window. It hides, and it shows, both at once. See you tomorrow.
